formReason: Get disk pages wrong and you would believe indexes speed up everything; get selectivity wrong and you would index every column; get write cost wrong and you would think indexes are free; get column order wrong and you would expect any filter to use it.
title: Why does an index only sometimes help?
hook: It saves page reads, nothing else
origin: The card lists what an index is, and its neighbours explain when it works

points.body: A lookup follows a few sorted pages instead of reading the table. If a scan reads few pages anyway, nothing is gained.
The sort order serves equality, ranges, and ORDER BY on its leading columns, and only those.
Every insert and update must also keep each index sorted, so an unused index is a pure cost.

anchor.line: The index at the back of a book
anchor.note: Worth it for one rare term; for a word on every page, you would just read the book.

card.a: A sorted tree of pages that lets the database find rows **without scanning the table**.

nodes.why: Reads are charged per page, not per row. Without this, a fast index looks like magic rather than arithmetic.
An index pays off only when it narrows the rows. A filter matching most of the table reads more pages through it.
A scan is not a failure. For small tables or broad filters it is the cheaper plan and the optimizer is right to choose it.
Each index is one more structure to update on every write, which is why adding one is a trade and not a free win.
An index on (a, b) is sorted by a first, so a filter on b alone finds no useful starting point.

shapes.title: The same rows, sorted
shapes.text: {1|The table} keeps rows in the order they arrived. {2|The index} is a second, sorted copy of one column that points back to them.
